**Given:** Finite dimensions $m\ge n\ge1$, integer $0\le k\le n$, $f\ge1$,
finite integer swap cap $S\ge0$, and the selected arithmetic mode. Exact
arithmetic includes exact scalar arithmetic, square roots of nonnegative
numbers, and comparisons as in the algorithm. Finite-precision components
are finite dyadic rationals, with exact rational arithmetic for the rank and
direct-certificate checks.

[F1] [[alg-strong-rank-revealing-qr-with-finite-swaps]]: the represented-input
rank test scans columns by exact elimination; QR uses finite local elimination
sweeps; a failed required operation returns a status; every repeated pass either
returns or consumes one of the $S$ swaps. Optional QR certification has a fixed
finite operation/refinement budget and otherwise returns `uncertified`.

[F2] [[alg-strong-rrqr-interpolative-decomposition]]: endpoint branches return
explicit matrices, nonsuccess is propagated without $J,T$, and success constructs
$T$ from a finite candidate $X$, exact identity entries, and a permutation.
The finite-precision direct check computes $(D,r^2,c^2)$ in exact rational
arithmetic and tests the listed entrywise conditions.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: for complex or real
vectors $u,v$, $|\langle u,v\rangle|^2\le\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2$.



1.1 In the rank test [F1], each of the $n$ columns scans at most $m$ rows. A nonzero pivot is the only divisor used in a row elimination, so every exact rational operation is defined and has finite integer numerators and denominators. Row swaps and subtracting a multiple of one row from another are invertible operations; they preserve all linear dependence relations among columns. At completion the echelon matrix has $r$ nonzero rows with distinct pivot columns, and all remaining rows vanish. Its pivot columns are independent by triangular back-substitution, and its image is contained in the $r$-dimensional space of vectors supported on the nonzero rows. Its rank is therefore exactly $r$, which equals the original rank. The same finite argument applies to the represented selected-block singularity test. Thus no rounded pivot threshold or undecidable limiting test is involved in either finite-precision rank decision. In exact mode the same rank-preserving operations and finite pivot scans apply over the exact input field, using the assumed exact arithmetic and comparisons. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Each QR initialization or refactorization has finitely many pivot scans and at most $mn$ local updates by [F1]. Their scalar operations terminate individually in the specified model. A zero target is skipped, and division is performed only after its denominator check. An inadmissible rounded operation exits with `range-failure`; a singular selected block exits with `singular-selected-block`. Otherwise triangular solves and inverse-row calculations use finitely many nonzero diagonal divisions, and finitely many norms and comparisons produce a score-test pass. In exact arithmetic the corresponding finite QR eliminations, norms, and comparisons are defined by the exact model; the same singular-block branch prevents an undefined solve. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Starting with zero swaps, every score-test pass either returns success, returns another nonsuccess status, or finds a violation. At a violation the procedure returns when the count is already $S$; otherwise it increments the count and repeats. Hence there are at most $S$ swaps and $S+1$ score-test passes. Each has finite work by step 2.1. The rank-deficient and $k=0$ QR branches return earlier. The optional QR certificate check uses only its fixed finite budget, so failure to certify cannot cause another unbounded loop or change a core status. The ordered exit branches assign exactly one core status. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The ID endpoint branches [F2] return after constructing finite empty or identity matrices. Every interior call terminates by step 3.1. Nonsuccess is propagated with both certificate statuses not applicable. On success the permutation determines distinct valid selected indices, and insertion and permutation of finitely many entries constructs $T$ in finite work. Every finite candidate entry is rational in the represented mode. Thus all entries of $D$, all squared moduli and their finite sum and maximum are exactly computable rationals, regardless of their magnitude; the symbolic square root $\sqrt{r^2}$ requires no rounded conversion. Identity and rational inequality checks terminate, assigning either `certified` or `uncertified`; endpoint certificate statuses are not required. This proves termination and well-definedness of all outputs and statuses. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 On an ID-certified branch the explicit checks [F2] give $T(:,J)=I_k$ and $c^2\le f^2$. Since $f\ge1$ and all moduli are nonnegative, $|T_{ab}|^2\le c^2\le f^2$ gives $|T_{ab}|\le f$. For every unit vector $x\in\mathbb F^n$, apply [F3] to each row of $D$ to obtain $|(Dx)_a|^2\le\sum_b|D_{ab}|^2$. Summing over rows gives $\|Dx\|_2^2\le\sum_{a,b}|D_{ab}|^2=r^2$. Taking the supremum over unit $x$ proves $\|D\|_2\le\sqrt{r^2}$ for the actual reconstruction residual. This uses only the direct exact data and no RRQR score certificate, as claimed. [F2, F3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice and real parameters $\alpha,\beta>-1$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: the Countable Choice axiom is assumed.

[F1] [[lem-real-power-lebesgue-integrability]]: for every $q>-1$, $x\mapsto x^q$ on $(0,1]$, extended by zero at zero, is nonnegative and Lebesgue integrable with integral $1/(q+1)$.

[F2] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] and [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]: under [A1], Borel sets in $[-1,1]$ lie in the Lebesgue sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure is a measure there; an interval has measure its length ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F3] [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], and [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]: positive-base powers are continuous, as are the finite products and compositions used in the density.

[F4] [[def-measure-with-density]]: a nonnegative measurable density $w$ defines the measure $w\,d\lambda$ by $E\mapsto\int_Ew\,d\lambda$.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval attains its finite minimum and maximum.

[F6] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and positively homogeneous.

[F7] [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]: bounded Riemann-integrable functions on compact intervals have the same Lebesgue integral under [A1]; [[thm-substitution]] gives the ordinary Riemann substitution on intervals away from the singular endpoints.

[F8] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] and [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]: increasing nonnegative measurable cutoffs have integrals increasing to the integral of their limit.

[F9] [[thm-riemann-criterion]]: a bounded function whose Darboux gaps can be made arbitrarily small is Riemann integrable.



1.1 The density is nonnegative and continuous on $(-1,1)$ by [F3]. For every real $c$, its strict superlevel is all of $[-1,1]$ when $c<0$, and the relatively open set $\{t\in(-1,1):w_{\alpha,\beta}(t)>c\}$ when $c\ge0$; thus the endpoint extension is Borel, and [F2] makes it Lebesgue measurable. Put $M_\alpha=\max(1,2^\alpha)$ and $M_\beta=\max(1,2^\beta)$. On $(-1,0]$ the factor $(1-t)^\alpha$ is at most $M_\alpha$, and on $[0,1)$ the factor $(1+t)^\beta$ is at most $M_\beta$. [A1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 To justify the endpoint integral comparisons, set $w_n=w_{\alpha,\beta}\chi_{[-1+1/n,1-1/n]}$ for $n\ge2$. Its superlevels are Borel by step 1.1. It is bounded and continuous except possibly at the two cutoff points; isolating these in intervals of arbitrarily small total length and using uniform continuity on the remaining compact pieces proves the Darboux criterion [F9]. The same argument applies to each half-interval restriction and to the corresponding power cutoffs. Consequently [F7] and the Riemann substitutions $u=1+t$ and $u=1-t$ give $\int_{-1}^0w_n\,d\lambda\le M_\alpha\int_{1/n}^1u^\beta\,d\lambda\le M_\alpha/(\beta+1)$ and $\int_0^1w_n\,d\lambda\le M_\beta\int_{1/n}^1u^\alpha\,d\lambda\le M_\beta/(\alpha+1)$, using [F1] and [F6] for the final bounds. Since $w_n\uparrow w_{\alpha,\beta}$ pointwise, including at the endpoints, [F8] gives $\int_{[-1,1]}w_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\lambda\le M_\alpha/(\beta+1)+M_\beta/(\alpha+1)<\infty$. [A1, F1, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], $\mu_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a positive Borel measure, and step 2.1 makes its total mass finite. If $U\subseteq[-1,1]$ is nonempty and relatively open, choose a nondegenerate closed interval $[c,d]\subset U\cap(-1,1)$. The density is continuous and strictly positive on $[c,d]$, so [F5] gives a minimum $m>0$ there. By [F2] and monotonicity [F6], $\mu_{\alpha,\beta}(U)\ge\int_{[c,d]}w_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\lambda\ge m(d-c)>0$. Therefore every point is in the relative support. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose]

4.1 For every $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $|t|^k\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, so [F6] gives $\int|t|^k\,d\mu_{\alpha,\beta}\le\mu_{\alpha,\beta}([-1,1])<\infty$ by step 2.1. This proves all moment claims. [F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** An open state domain $G$, a $C^3$ flux $f:G\to\mathbb R^m$, a state
$\bar u\in G$ at which $Df(\bar u)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues, and an
index $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.

[F1] [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]: $A=Df$ is $C^2$; genuine nonlinearity means $D\lambda_i r_i$ is nonzero and has constant sign after shrinking the neighborhood.

[F2] [[def-rankine-hugoniot-and-lax-shocks]]: a strict Lax $i$-shock satisfies $[f]=s[u]$ and the ordered family inequalities.

[F3] [[lem-smooth-simple-characteristic-eigenpairs]]: near a state with $m$
distinct real eigenvalues, local $C^2$ ordered eigenpairs exist and their
eigenvectors form a basis.

[F4] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]]: a $C^1$ equation with invertible derivative in the unknowns has a unique local $C^1$ solution.

[F5] [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.



1.1 On a neighborhood where [F3] supplies the $C^2$ right-eigenvector frame, let $R(u)$ have columns $r_j(u)$ and let $\ell_i(u)^T$ be row $i$ of $R(u)^{-1}$. Then $R^{-1}A=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_j)R^{-1}$, so $\ell_i^Tr_j=\delta_{ij}$ and $\ell_i$ is a left eigenvector. For $v$ near $r_i(\bar u)$ define $G(u_0,\sigma,v,s)=\left(\int_0^1 Df(u_0+t\sigma v)v\,dt-sv,\;\ell_i(u_0)\cdot v-1\right)$. Since $Df$ is $C^2$, this $G$ is $C^1$ in all variables and vanishes at $(\bar u,0,r_i(\bar u),\lambda_i(\bar u))$. [given, F1, F3, construct]

1.2 Shrink the base neighborhood to an open ball $N_0$ whose closure $K$ lies inside the IFT parameter neighborhood, and choose $\eta>0$ so $K\times[-\eta,\eta]$ lies there. By continuity and the nonzero value of $d_i(\bar u)$, shrink $K$ so $|d_i(u_0)|$ and all eigenvalue gaps have positive lower bounds on $K$. The $C^1$ functions $(u_0,\sigma)\mapsto\lambda_i(S_i(\sigma;u_0))$ and $s_i(\sigma,u_0)$ have uniformly continuous $\sigma$ derivatives on the compact product $K\times[-\eta,\eta]$ by [F5]. Their first-order expansions at $\sigma=0$ therefore have uniform remainders over $u_0\in K$:

2.1 The derivative of $G$ in $(v,s)$ at that point sends $(w,\alpha)$ to $((A(\bar u)-\lambda_i I)w-\alpha r_i(\bar u),\ell_i(\bar u)\cdot w)$. If it vanishes, pairing the first component with $\ell_i(\bar u)$ gives $\alpha=0$; simplicity then makes $w$ a multiple of $r_i(\bar u)$, and the last component forces $w=0$. Hence this square derivative is invertible. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F4] with parameter $(u_0,\sigma)$ and unknowns $(v,s)$. It gives unique $C^1$ functions $v_i(\sigma,u_0),s_i(\sigma,u_0)$ on a product neighborhood. Set $S_i(\sigma;u_0)=u_0+\sigma v_i(\sigma,u_0)$. For $\sigma\ne0$, multiplying the first equation by $\sigma$ and using the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $f(S_i(\sigma;u_0))-f(u_0)=s_i(\sigma,u_0)(S_i(\sigma;u_0)-u_0)$. At $\sigma=0$, the unique normalized eigenvector is $v_i(0,u_0)=r_i(u_0)$; hence $\partial_\sigma S_i(0;u_0)=r_i(u_0)$. [step 2.1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 At any fixed $u_0\in N_0$, differentiate the first component of $G=0$ at $\sigma=0$. It gives $(A(u_0)-\lambda_i I)\partial_\sigma v_i(0,u_0)+\tfrac12D^2f(u_0)[r_i,r_i]-\partial_\sigma s_i(0,u_0)r_i=0$. Pairing with $\ell_i(u_0)$ yields $\partial_\sigma s_i(0,u_0)=\tfrac12\ell_i(u_0)\cdot D^2f(u_0)[r_i,r_i]=\tfrac12D\lambda_i(u_0)r_i(u_0)$; the last equality follows by differentiating $Ar_i=\lambda_i r_i$ in direction $r_i$ and pairing with $\ell_i$. [step 3.1, F3, algebra]
$$\lambda_i(S_i(\sigma;u_0))=\lambda_i(u_0)+\sigma d_i(u_0)+o(|\sigma|),\qquad s_i(\sigma,u_0)=\lambda_i(u_0)+\tfrac12\sigma d_i(u_0)+o(|\sigma|).$$
For $\sigma d_i(u_0)<0$ and sufficiently small uniform $|\sigma|$, this gives $\lambda_i(S_i(\sigma;u_0))<s_i(\sigma,u_0)<\lambda_i(u_0)$. The other-family inequalities in [F2] follow by continuity from the positive gaps, after shrinking $N_0$ and $\eta$. [step 4.1, F1, F2, F5, algebra, choose] ∎

**Given:** AC, the explicit regular companion geometry, $1<p<\infty$, the mean interpolator and zero boundary cell-face vectors.

[F1] [[def-fv-regular-simplicial-companion-family]] gives $|K|\asymp h^d$, $|F|\asymp h^{d-1}$, $d_{K,F}\asymp h$, shape-regular simplex maps, and uniformly bounded vertex-star paths.

[F2] [[thm-reference-simplex-trace-and-gauss-green]] and [[thm-reference-simplex-poincare-wirtinger]] give the $W^{1,p}$ face trace, Gauss–Green and mean-zero Poincaré inequalities. Affine rescaling gives on a subdivision simplex $S$ and facet $e$ the bounds $\|z\|_{L^p(e)}\le C(h^{-1/p}\|z\|_{L^p(S)}+h^{1-1/p}\|\nabla z\|_{L^p(S)})$ and $\|z-z_S\|_{L^p(S)}\le Ch\|\nabla z\|_{L^p(S)}$.

[F3] [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]] defines $G_K$ and $\rho_{K,F}$; its face-moment identities hold for actual polytopes by applying simplex Gauss–Green to constants and coordinate functions and cancelling subdivision facets.

[F4] [[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]] bounds $\|w\|_p$ by $\|\nabla w\|_p$ for $w\in W_0^{1,p}$; [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the continuous $W_0^{1,p}\to L^2$ inclusion on the strict stated branch. Finite-sum and integral Hölder inequalities are [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]].



1.1 Write $j_{K,F}=v_F-v_K$. The moment cancellation gives $G_Kv=|K|^{-1}\sum_F|F|j_{K,F}n_{K,F}$. Hölder, the bounded face count and [F1] imply $|K||G_Kv|^p\le C\sum_Fh^{d-p}|j_{K,F}|^p$. Since $\rho_{K,F}=j_{K,F}-G_Kv\cdot(x_F-x_K)$ and $|x_F-x_K|\le Ch$, summing gives $B_{h,p}\le CD_{h,p}$. Conversely $j_{K,F}=\rho_{K,F}+G_Kv\cdot(x_F-x_K)$ gives $D_{h,p}\le CB_{h,p}$. [F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 If $K,L$ share $F$, $v_K-v_L=j_{L,F}-j_{K,F}$. Along a supplied vertex-star path, the difference between $v_K$ and any other incident cell value is a sum of at most $2J$ such increments. At a boundary vertex the same telescoping ends at a zero boundary face. Hence for every simplex $S\subset\overline K$ and its vertex $z$, $|(E_hv)(z)-v_K|^p\le C\sum_{(L,F)\in\mathcal N(K)}|j_{L,F}|^p$, where $\mathcal N(K)$ is the union of the finitely many supplied paths at its vertices. These sets have bounded cardinality and bounded overlap: a cell has at most $J(d+1)$ subdivision vertices and each vertex has at most $J$ incident cells. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 The scaled simplex estimates [F2] first bound the difference between the mean on a simplex and the mean on one of its facets by $Ch^{1-d/p}\|\nabla z\|_{L^p(S)}$. Means on adjacent simplices differ by the sum of their differences to the shared facet mean, since their traces agree. The fan subdivision is a connected finite union of at most $J$ simplices. Telescoping between their means, and averaging over each original cell or original face, therefore gives $|(I_hz)_F-(I_hz)_K|^p\le Ch^{p-d}\int_K|\nabla z|^p$. The same trace argument applies to boundary faces; zero-boundary approximation makes their means zero. Multiplication by $|F|d_{K,F}^{1-p}\asymp h^{d-p}$ and summation proves $D_{h,p}(I_hz)\le C\|\nabla z\|_p$. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

1.4 For smooth $z$, Gauss–Green gives $G_KI_hz=|K|^{-1}\int_K\nabla z$ exactly. On each cell Taylor expansion around its centroid and the corresponding face averages show $|(I_hz)_F-(I_hz)_K-G_KI_hz\cdot(x_F-x_K)|\le Ch^2\|D^2z\|_\infty$ under the stated centroid hypothesis. Thus for this mean interpolator the residual sum is at most $C h^p\|D^2z\|_\infty^p$, because there are $O(h^{-d})$ cells. Uniform continuity of $\nabla z$ gives the asserted gradient consistency. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Barycentric coordinates on $S$ have absolute value at most one and gradients at most $C/h$, by the inradius bound. Applying step 1.2 to $E_hv-v_K$ gives its $p$th-power $L^p(S)$ norm at most $Ch^d$ times the path sum, and its gradient norm at most $Ch^{d-p}$ times that sum. Summing with bounded overlap proves $\|E_hv-\Pi_hv\|_p\le ChD_{h,p}$ and $\|\nabla E_hv\|_p\le CD_{h,p}$. The continuous piecewise affine function vanishes on all boundary facets. Its zero extension is globally Lipschitz and has compact support: along a segment, the finite simplex pieces and the exterior zero pieces have derivative bounded by the largest simplex gradient and agree at crossings. To verify the zero-boundary closure directly, multiply by $\max(0,\min(1,k\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)-1))$. The error and its gradient are supported in shrinking boundary layers, and $|E_hv(x)|\le L\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ bounds the cutoff-gradient term by $2L$ on the layer $1/k<\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)<2/k$. They tend to zero in $W^{1,p}$ by absolute continuity of the integral. Each cutoff is Lipschitz with compact support in $\Omega$ and can be mollified inside $\Omega$, producing smooth compactly supported approximants. Thus $E_hv\in W_0^{1,p}$, and [F4] proves the full $W^{1,p}$ bound and the $L^p$ state bound. [F1, F4, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 For $p<2$, the same barycentric estimate in $L^2(S)$ and $\ell^2\le\ell^p$ for the combined finite coefficient list give $\|E_hv-\Pi_hv\|_2\le Ch^{d/2}(\sum_{K,F}|j_{K,F}|^p)^{1/p}\le Ch^{1+d/2-d/p}D_{h,p}$. For $p\ge2$, finite-measure Hölder and step 2.1 give $ChD_{h,p}$ instead. The exponent is positive precisely on the stated strict branch. The continuous embedding [F4] bounds $\|E_hv\|_2$, proving the state $L^2$ estimate as well. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $\phi_K$ and $\phi_F$ denote vector means over cells and faces. Gauss–Green, shared face cancellation and $v_F=0$ on the boundary give exactly $\int G_hv\cdot\phi+\Pi_hv\operatorname{div}\phi=\sum_{K,F}|F|j_{K,F}n_{K,F}\cdot(\phi_K-\phi_F)$. Since $|\phi_K-\phi_F|\le Ch\|\nabla\phi\|_\infty$, Hölder bounds this by $ChD_{h,p}(\sum_{K,F}|F|d_{K,F})^{1/p'}\|\nabla\phi\|_\infty$. The last sum is uniformly bounded by [F1], proving the estimate. Strong and weak convergence pass its left side to $\int g\cdot\phi+v\operatorname{div}\phi$, which is zero; interior compactly supported tests identify $g=\nabla v$. Hölder in time gives the same assertions for space-time bounds. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega^-$, and $u\in E^+(\Omega^+)$. Choose $R$ so large that $\overline{\Omega^-}\subset B_{R/4}$ and set $A=\Omega^+\cap B_R$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed through Poincare–Wirtinger and Countable Choice through polar slicing ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Poincare–Wirtinger controls the mean-zero part of an H1 function on a bounded connected extension domain ([[thm-poincare-wirtinger-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains]]).

[F2] The trace theorem bounds the H1/2 trace on $\Gamma$ by the H1 norm in a bounded exterior collar ([[lem-bem-lipschitz-trace-and-lifting]]).

[F3] Tonelli/Fubini applies after the actual polar measure formula in [F90], including to nonnegative squared Sobolev derivatives. ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]])

[F90] Polar integration uses the published radial formula, not a linear substitution: $dx=r^{n-1}dr\,d\sigma(\omega)$. The sphere measure agrees with graph-chart surface measure and scales by $R^{n-1}$. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]])

[F4] The already assumed AC supplies bounded $H^1$ extension on every bounded Lipschitz domain, connected or not, by [[lem-na-lipschitz-scalar-h1-h2-extension]]. After a bounded-support cutoff, approximate identities converge in $L^2$ for the extension and each first derivative, and convolution commutes with those derivatives. Thus ambient smooth restrictions are $H^1$ dense on bounded annuli. ([[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]], [[prop-mollifier-families-are-l-one-approximate-identities]], [[thm-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-in-l-p]], [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]])

[F5] A one-dimensional $H^1$ class on a bounded interval has an absolutely continuous representative with its weak derivative as derivative, and that representative obeys the fundamental theorem; AC supplies the CC/DC hypotheses of the cited theorem. The one-dimensional Sobolev-to-AC identification is the $n=1$ ACL characterization; completeness is the Sobolev Banach theorem. ([[thm-acl-characterisation-of-w-one-p]]) ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]], [[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]])



1.1 We justify the Sobolev slices. On each bounded spherical shell $a<|x|<b$ with $R/2<a<R<b$, $u$ belongs to $H^1$: bounded volume and $L^6$ give $L^2$, and its weak gradient is already $L^2$. Use [F4] to approximate it by ambient smooth $u_m$ in $H^1$ on a slightly larger shell. The polar formula [F90] and $a^2\le r^2\le b^2$ bound $\int_{S^2}\|u_m(r\omega)-u_l(r\omega)\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2d\sigma(\omega)$ by $C\|u_m-u_l\|_{H^1}^2$, because the radial derivative of a smooth approximant is $\omega\cdot\nabla u_m$. Take a subsequence with summable successive $H^1$ errors; Cauchy–Schwarz on the finite angular measure and Tonelli show that the successive slice norms are summable for almost every $\omega$. Completeness [F5] gives an $H^1(a,b)$ slice limit, identified by the polar $L^2$ limit with $u(r\omega)$ and derivative $\omega\cdot\nabla u(r\omega)$. Countably many overlapping shells exhaust $r>R/2$, so their representatives agree on overlaps off one angular null set; their values at $R$ define the usual trace, since the one-dimensional $H^1$ endpoint estimate passes smooth approximants to that value. By [F5] the slices are locally absolutely continuous. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F90, given, construct]

2.1 For almost every direction $\omega\in S^2$, the radial slice $r\mapsto u(r\omega)$ is locally H1 for $r\ge R$, and $\int_R^\infty|u(r\omega)|^6r^2dr<\infty$. Thus there is a sequence $r_m\to\infty$ with $u(r_m\omega)\to0$. For each such direction the radial derivative is square integrable with weight $r^2$; the one-dimensional fundamental theorem on $[R,r_m]$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|u(R\omega)|^2\le\left(\int_R^\infty|\partial_ru(r\omega)|^2r^2dr\right)\left(\int_R^\infty r^{-2}dr\right)=R^{-1}\int_R^\infty|\partial_ru(r\omega)|^2r^2dr.$ Integrating over $S^2$ by [F3,F90] yields $\|u\|_{L^2(\partial B_R)}\le R^{1/2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega^+\setminus B_R)}$. [A1, F3, F5, F90, step 1.1, given, choose]

3.1 The bounded annular domain $A=\Omega^+\cap B_R$ is Lipschitz: its boundary components are the original Lipschitz $\Gamma$ and the separated smooth sphere. Hence [F4] gives the exact extension-domain property required by [F1]. It is connected: for any point inside $B_{R/2}$, path-connectivity of the unbounded open set $\Omega^+$ gives a path to a point outside $B_{R/2}$; stopping at the first crossing of $\partial B_{R/2}$ keeps the path in $A$. The sphere $\partial B_{R/2}$ lies wholly in $A$ and is connected, and the outer shell $R/2<|x|<R$ is connected, so all points of $A$ join within $A$. Put $m=|A|^{-1}\int_Au$.
